blindSummary: No region-specific incident, enforcement or ordinance evidence was found; this state/province sits within ordinary national compliance: a 2019 reform of the civil-registry law created an administrative legal-gender-recognition procedure, with implementing regulations set by gubernatorial decree.
blindSourceSummaries: NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy); an international human-rights organisation's news backgrounder (31 March 2025) on progress and challenges for trans rights in this country - the dossier cites it for the count that 22 of 32 states/provinces had legislated a legal gender-recognition procedure by March 2025, and for the per-unit compliance picture.

NOTE: page not retrievable at fetch time (no cached copy); an international human-rights organisation's report (6 March 2024) on the need for legal gender recognition in another state/province of the country - it documents that the absence of any gender-recognition procedure exposes trans people to police and institutional mistreatment, co-authored with a local trans community organisation; the dossier cites it as the clearest case among the six states/provinces whose legislatures still refuse any procedure.

A newspaper report (24 July 2024) on the country's capital making transfeminicide a crime with sentences of up to 70 years (a transfeminicide statute named for a trans sex worker murdered in 2016 whose attacker was released after 48 hours despite footage and witnesses and has been on the run since): the capital is the second of the country's 32 states/provinces to criminalise transfeminicide - earlier in 2024 another small coastal state/province introduced sentences of up to 60 years for the crime; the law also lets victims' friends, not only relatives, claim bodies and drive investigations, which matters where families disown trans relatives; it lands against more than 95% impunity for homicides in the country in 2022, believed higher for transfeminicides.
